candidates.source_description:
**Mędrcy** - 2 figury z cyklu “Mędrcy” stworzone przez Magdalenę Abakanowicz w latach 1987–88

**Materiał:** tkanina jutowa utwardzana żywicą, postumenty metalowe
**Wymiary figur:** wysokość 112 centymetrów, szerokość 55 centymetry oraz głębokość 67 centymetry  
**Wymiary postumentów:** wysokość 96 centymetrów, szerokość 52 centymetrów oraz głębokość 43 centymetry 
Dzieło ze zbiorów Muzeum Narodowego we Wrocławiu prezentowane na wystawie stałej w Pawilonie Czterech Kopuł. Dzieło zostało przekazane przez artystkę muzeum w 1990 roku. 2 Figury z cyklu Mędrcy autorstwa Magdaleny Abakanowicz zostały wykonane z tkaniny jutowej utwardzonej żywicą. Figury Mędrców wykonane są z jednego odlewu, w którym  artystka umieszczała fragmenty tkaniny pozyskiwanej z używanych worków jutowych. Wcześniej płótno workowe moczyła w kleju stolarskim, następnie je w tym gipsowym odlewie układała i dociskała, a na końcu utwardzane żywicą syntetyczną.
evidence: Museum object article and its own Sketchfab publisher agree on artist, title, 1987–1988, resin-hardened jute, two distinct metal pedestals, and figure dimensions. Museum notes donation by artist in 1990. A later museum announcement documents the pair on a three-year Luxembourg loan from May 2025.

candidates.source_description:
Carmela is one of four sculptures by Jaume Plensa which were exhibited at the Palau de la Musica Catalana in 2016.
The statue was such a hit with the neighbours that they started a petition on change.org asking the organizers and Barcelona city council to keep it there indefinitely. Carmela was created from a photo of a Barcelona teenager. Plensa scanned the photo to create a three dimensional image which he then compressed in one axes before casting it in iron.

The result is an enigmatic flattened sculpture which, when viewed from the right angle, looks like a large three-dimensional bust.

candidates.note: A physical relief/assemblage scan, distinct from Atrium’s public Saint Phalle fountain figures and Nikigator. candidates.source_description:
*Shooting Picture* is a relief work by the artist Niki de Saint Phalle. The surface of the work is rough and textured, featuring a white background and multiple streams of differently coloured paint including purple, yellow, blue, red and black. Each of the colours appears to have dripped down the canvas from a hole, which exposes a dark surface beneath the white. Saint Phalle made this work by shooting with a gun at bags of paint that were placed on the canvas. Before the shooting began, the surface was covered with white plaster and pigment to resemble a blank canvas. As the shooting commenced, the bags would be punctured and the coloured paints released to flow and splash.

Captured with Samsung Note 8, processed with Recap Photo using 38 photos.
evidence: Stedelijk’s 2017 restoration appendix lists Saint Phalle’s Tir (Shooting Altar), 1970. Its official Heart Tour also identifies the title. Publisher names the same Stedelijk object and documents capture using 38 Samsung Note 8 photographs, processed in ReCap Photo.

candidates.source_description:
Paolozzi studied at the Edinburgh College of Art in 1943 and at the Slade School of Fine Art, London, 1944-47.
In 1947-49 he spent time in Paris and became involved with Surrealism and Dubuffet's Art Brut. His collages from magazines and brochures made him a co-founder of English Pop Art.
Paolozzi formed sculptures and sculptures from scrap, found objects and high-quality material, which deal with the theme of machine aesthetics.
Paolozzi's intention with this work is not to illustrate Bruckner's music, but - in a completely independent manner - to set a comparable counterpoint in the pictorial. (P. Baum)
evidence: Lentos describes the 1977 forum metall sculpture, its placement by Paolozzi, cast iron, and fabrication by VOEST. The city’s Donaupark brochure identifies Hommage à Anton Bruckner, 1977, cast iron, Austrian Ludwig Foundation loan, and states the forum metall works were designed for Linz and made in Austrian industrial firms.

candidates.source_description:
Born in Rosario, Argentina, **Lucio Fontana** (1899-1968) lived and worked in Italy, where he became one of the most important artists of the 20th Century. Known for the slashes paintings (the “spatial concepts” series), Fontana was the creator of Spatialism, with which he looked for a third dimension in painting.
He was also a prolific sculptor with his interest turned on by classical art and by materials such as ceramics and gold. Paolo Chinelli Funeral Monument is one of the best examples in Fontana’s sculpture at the Monumental Cemetery in Milan. It represents a strange angelic creature, maybe inspired by Nike of Samotracia, that appears as though floating in the air, inside a concrete cube.

More info at [Monumental Cemetery of Milan Website](http://https://monumentale.comune.milano.it/monumenti/monumento-chinelli)
evidence: Cemetery’s official itinerary identifies Chinelli Monument, architect Renzo Zavanella, sculptor Lucio Fontana, 1949, and exact position. Its Fontana page identifies the ceramic figure. Visionaria archive describes the jointly created 1949 tomb’s granite frame and suspended ceramic sculpture; model publisher identifies this exact monument and niche.
